newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE euroyen slides to end just off day's low.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE euroyen slides to end just off day's low.

text.p: The key March three-month TIFFE euroyen futures contract slid to end Tokyo trade on Tuesday just off its day's low as a variety of factors contributed to a gradual increase in bearish sentiment, traders said.

Sales of fixed interest rates, weakness in Japanese government bond futures and comments from Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara all helped push the March down. It settled at 98.96 against 99.01 on Monday.
March moved from 98.95 to 99.00, with volume of 64,760 contracts traded, and one trader with a trust bank's securities arm said further sales could result should the key contract slip below 98.95.

Others agreed that March is growing vulnerable. "Sentiment is gradually getting darker, and people appear to be lightening their positions in both fixed interest rates and euroyen futures," one trust bank trader said.
Although the March had been edging lower throughout the day, the downside managed to hold near 98.97 until just after Japanese government bond (JGB) trading closed.

The key September JGB contract closed at 124.75, near the day's low of 124.73, compared with Monday's 124.96. Traders attributed the slip to strong 4.5 percent month-on-month growth in revised May industrial output, along with a foreign media report saying Sakakibara, newly appointed MOF vice minister, said market views on the economy are still too pessimistic.
Euroyen traders were divided on how much direct impact Sakakibara's statements on their market, but said that this had given traders a handy excuse for lightening their positions.
Wariness about potential Sakakibara statements at a 0930 GMT news conference also kept the topside weighted.
In the interest rate swap (IRS) market, rates rose across the board as operators, mainly Japanese banks, lightened their positions, helping undercut euroyen futures, traders said.

Two-year IRS rates were quoted at 1.14/18 percent in late afternoon, up from 1.10/14 percent on Monday, while 10-year IRS rates were quoted at 2.77/81 percent against 2.74/78 percent. But traders said such rises were unlikely to continue.

An additional negative factor was the afternoon announcement that the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan (LTCB) and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) had signed a letter of intent to form a global strategic alliance.
Traders said this could ease concerns about instability in the Japanese financial system and might help boost the Nikkei stock index on Wednesday by prompting buying of financial sector stocks.

The Bank of Japan (BOJ) injected 200 billion yen into the money market in the face of a 190 billion yen shortfall, as expected by the market. Traders said the weighted average of the key overnight call rate was likely to be 0.51 percent, the same as Monday, although it was also being traded at 0.52 percent. Most activity was position adjustment in connection with today being the last day of the current reserve period.

No three-month certificates of deposit (CDs) were issued, although they were offered at 0.66 percent, unchanged from Monday. But around 12 billion yen of one-month CDs was issued at 0.59 percent and 50 billion yen of two-month CDs at 0.60 percent.
Two-month CDs were last issued on July 3 at 0.61 percent, although they were offered on Monday at 0.60 percent.
